original_item.title: Verify withdrawal proof uses Groth16 verification with correct inputs

counterexample.description: Attempt to teleport with forged Groth16 proof
preconditions: Attacker crafts proof with arbitrary pubSignals
attack_steps: 1. Craft invalid proof with desired transferRoot, recipient, value
counterexample.expected_behavior: Groth16 verification fails, tx reverts with InvalidProof
counterexample.result: COUNTEREXAMPLE_REFUTED - ZK soundness prevents proof forgery

reviewed_items.reasoning: The withdrawal proof verification is correctly implemented with two distinct paths: (1) Nova proofs via teleport() at line 312-329 using IWithdrawDecider.verifyOpaqueNovaProof(), and (2) Groth16 proofs via singleTeleport() at line 337-351 using IWithdrawVerifier.verifyProof(). Both paths enforce verification BEFORE any state modification or token minting. The public inputs are correctly extracted: for Nova (proof_[1]=transferRoot, proof_[2]=recipient, proof_[8]=totalValue) and for Groth16 (pubSignals[0]=transferRoot, pubSignals[1]=recipient, pubSignals[2]=totalValue). The cryptographic binding of these public inputs ensures proof forgery is computationally infeasible under the discrete log assumption.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexample assumes an attacker can craft a valid Groth16 proof for arbitrary public inputs. This is computationally infeasible as it would require breaking the discrete logarithm problem or finding a collision in the BN254 pairing. The ZK soundness property guarantees that only valid proofs (corresponding to valid private witness) will be accepted.

guards_found.reason: require(IWithdrawDecider(withdrawDecider).verifyOpaqueNovaProof(proof_), InvalidProof()) - verification MUST pass before _teleport() is called
require(IWithdrawVerifier(singleWithdrawVerifier).verifyProof(pA, pB, pC, pubSignals), InvalidProof()) - Groth16 verification enforced
abi.decode enforces correct proof structure; malformed proofs fail at decode

original_item.title: Verify teleport delta calculation is correct

counterexample.description: Attempt to mint more than delta

reviewed_items.reasoning: The delta calculation in _teleport() is mathematically correct and protected against overflow/underflow. At line 377-380: currentTotal is read from storage, the require(value > currentTotal) ensures the subtraction cannot underflow, diff = value - currentTotal computes the correct delta, and totalTeleported[recipient] += diff updates the counter. The Solidity 0.8.33 compiler provides built-in overflow/underflow protection. The sequence is: (1) read current total, (2) validate value > current, (3) compute diff, (4) update storage, (5) mint tokens. This ensures exactly the delta is minted and the cumulative model is maintained.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexample describes the expected correct behavior, not an attack. The arithmetic is straightforward: diff = 100 - 30 = 70. The proof value (100) represents cumulative amount, currentTotal (30) represents already claimed, so the delta (70) is the new amount to mint. This is correct behavior, not a vulnerability.

guards_found.reason: require(value > currentTotal, NothingToWithdraw(currentTotal, value)) - ensures diff will be positive and prevents replay
diff = value - currentTotal - underflow impossible due to prior require; Solidity 0.8+ provides overflow protection
$.totalTeleported[recipient] += diff - atomic update before external call

original_item.title: Verify STATE-TELEPORT-COMPLETE requires all validations passed

preconditions: Valid proof, valid root, valid recipient, value > currentTotal
attack_steps: 2. Any validation failure should prevent minting
counterexample.expected_behavior: All validations must pass before mint
counterexample.actual_behavior: Sequential requires enforce ordering; any failure reverts entire tx

reviewed_items.reasoning: The _teleport() function enforces a strict validation sequence where all checks must pass before token minting occurs. The execution order is: (1) root validation at lines 367-369, (2) recipient hash validation at lines 372-373, (3) chain ID validation at lines 374-375, (4) monotonicity check at line 378, (5) state update at line 380, (6) token minting at line 382, (7) event emission at line 383. Each require() statement uses Solidity's revert semantics, which atomically rolls back all state changes on failure. The EVM's transaction atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing execution. No partial state is possible.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexample describes attempting to reach token minting without passing all validations. This is impossible due to sequential require statements in Solidity - each require MUST pass before the next line executes. Any failure reverts the entire transaction with no state changes.

guards_found.reason: Root validation: require(expectedRoot != 0) and require(expectedRoot == transferRoot)
EVM guarantees all-or-nothing execution; revert rolls back entire transaction

Verifier.sol:382 - IzERC20($.token).teleport() - minting only after ALL checks pass
Verifier.sol:383 - emit Teleport(...) - event after successful mint

original_item.title: Verify teleport rejection provides proper error indication

counterexample.actual_behavior: Custom errors include failing values for debugging

reviewed_items.reasoning: The teleport rejection error handling is comprehensive and provides clear diagnostic information. Each failure mode has a distinct custom error with relevant parameters: InvalidProof() at lines 326/348, ExpectedRootZero(rootHint) at line 368, TransferRootMismatch(expected, actual) at line 369, RecipientMismatch(expected, actual) at line 373, InvalidRecipientChainId(provided, expected) at line 375, and NothingToWithdraw(currentTotal, value) at line 378. All errors are declared at lines 50-68 with descriptive names and typed parameters. Solidity's revert semantics ensure no silent failures - all require() statements propagate errors and roll back state atomically.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: This is not a vulnerability counterexample but a code quality assertion about error handling clarity. The assertion is verified - all failure modes have distinct, parameterized custom errors that provide actionable debugging information.

guards_found.reason: All errors are explicitly declared with typed parameters for debugging
Every require uses a descriptive custom error, no bare require() or assert()

original_item.title: Verify root relay uses correct LayerZero encoding and destination

counterexample.description: Attempt to relay to wrong destination
counterexample.expected_behavior: Message always sent to $.hubEid (immutable after init)
counterexample.actual_behavior: hubEid read from storage, set in __Verifier_init

reviewed_items.reasoning: The relayTransferRoot() function at lines 393-413 correctly implements LayerZero message relay to the Hub. The destination hubEid is set during initialization at line 223 ($.hubEid = hubEid_) and read from storage at line 405 for _quote() and implicitly at line 409 for _lzSend(). The payload encoding at line 404 uses abi.encode(root, index) which is deterministic and matches the Hub's expected TRANSFER_PAYLOAD_LENGTH = 64 bytes (uint256 root + uint64 index padded to 256 bits). The function enforces: (1) whenNotPaused modifier, (2) root exists check at line 402, (3) fee validation at line 406. The latestRelayedIndex is updated at line 412 only after successful _lzSend(). The destination cannot be manipulated by callers.

counterexample_evaluation.assessment: The counterexample assumes an attacker could redirect the relay to a wrong destination. This is not possible because hubEid is set at initialization (owner-controlled) and stored immutably in contract storage. The relayTransferRoot function reads hubEid from storage and passes it to _lzSend - callers cannot specify an alternative destination.

guards_found.reason: $.hubEid = hubEid_ - set once at init, no setter function exists
require(root != 0, NoProvedRoot()) - prevents relay of empty root
abi.encode(root, index) - deterministic encoding matching Hub expectations
